items.title: ARTEX abuse expands as cybercriminals target financial sector
items.summary: In this article Mitigation and protection guidance Microsoft Defender detections Hunting queries Indicators of compromise In October 2026, the financially motivated threat actor Storm-3358 began targeting organizations in the financial sector using the agentic AI offensive framework ARTEX. The threat actor that Microsoft Threat Intelligence tracks as Storm-3358 is a Cambodia-based intrusion cluster that primarily targets financial organizations in Southeast Asia, in addition to a smaller number of large financial organizations globally. Microsoft has observed Storm-3358 use ARTEX in combination with conventional automated tools to scan systems connected to the public internet, exploit security flaws including anonymous file upload and server-side request forgery (SSRF), and install open-source remote access trojans (RATs). Storm-3358 has used the WISP, vshell, and AdaptixC2 RATs for persistence and lateral movement. Microsoft has observed ARTEX agents using utilities like netcat and curl to download these RATs to compromised systems, as shown in Figure 1. Figure 1. Example commands that ARTEX agents used to download RATs to compromised systems. In recent ARTEX-related attacks, threat actors have used ARTEX agents to scan and exploit vulnerabilities in web applications, use web shells for persistence on compromised web servers, compromise credentials from public sources and compromised systems, and use compromised cloud identities for persistence and data exfiltration. ARTEX agents can also perform brute-force password attacks, password spraying, API enumeration and abuse, and database dumping. Agentic tools like ARTEX can leverage compromised credentials and systems at machine speed to move laterally, escalate privileges, and exfiltrate data. This activity illustrates an ongoing trend of threat actors accelerating all stages of the attack chain with agentic AI penetration testing frameworks, including ARTEX. As these capabilities evolve, defenders must similarly use AI to investigate and respond across large environments. While threat actors regularly use proxies and virtual private networks (VPNs) to change the source IP address of malicious traffic and bypass static detections, Microsoft is providing indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help defenders detect related activity. Mitigation and protection guidance Microsoft’s research into threats involving agentic frameworks informs security detections and investigative context across its products. The capabilities available to customers depend on the source of the activity and the products and protections deployed in their environment. Several behavioral signals can help organizations determine that they are being targeted by threat actors using agentic AI. Agentic AI frameworks scanning a target send a wide variety of requests in a brief time and retry variations on the same technique or move on to next-stage actions at machine speed. Agentic AI frameworks use existing penetration testing tools. For example, ARTEX by default uses Nmap, curl, wget, Python HTTP clients, Norma SDK WebFetch, and headless Chromium through Playwright, among others. These tools may send network traffic with distinctive characteristics, such as default user agent strings. While blocking network traffic with these characteristics will not stop an attack by an AI agent, which will quickly change them, identifying them can alert defenders to the activity. Defensive honeypots , decoys, tarpits, and fake wins can pull autonomous AI attacks away from legitimate targets. Honeypots and decoy surfaces such as Microsoft Sentinel Deception give the agent attractive but worthless targets to pursue. Tarpits consume the agent’s time and budget. Fake wins present convincing evidence that the agent’s objective is complete, which can cause it to stop on a false success. In Microsoft’s testing, these controls helped reduce the attack traffic reaching real assets and produced high-confidence, attribution-quality signal. For additional information on the evolution of threat actors’ use of ARTEX please see Microsoft’s recent blogs: AI-driven, large-scale nation-state campaign using ARTEX enables supply chain compromise and Threat actors use agentic AI tooling to find and abuse exposed secrets . Microsoft’s continuous research into threat actors leveraging agentic frameworks integrates directly into the following products: Identity and sign-in activity — Microsoft Entra ID Protection Microsoft analyzes sign-in activity and other signals to identify potential identity risk. Customers can investigate risk detections and risky sign-ins, and configure Conditional Access policies that use sign-in or user risk to require multifactor authentication or block access when specified conditions are met. Identity and sign-in activity from known threat actor infrastructure, including from agentic frameworks like ARTEX, generate Verified threat actor IP risk detections delivered at high risk. See: Investigate risk with Microsoft Entra ID Protection Risk-based user sign-in protection in Microsoft Entra ID What are risk detections? – Microsoft Entra ID Protection Endpoint activity — Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Endpoint alerts help security teams identify and investigate suspicious activity on devices. Indicators of compromise can support detection and, when configured, blocking. Customers can review related alerts in the Microsoft Defender portal. See: Review alerts in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Activity across security domains — Microsoft Defender portal The portal brings together alerts and incidents from Microsoft security solutions and provides relevant threat intelligence to support investigation, threat hunting, and response. This helps customers assess suspicious activity in the context of their own environment. See: Investigate alerts in Microsoft Defender XDR Security Dashboard for AI Threat actor misuse of AI accelerates risk across enterprise environments by amplifying existing threats such as exploitation of vulnerabilities, phishing, malware threats, and insider activity. To help organizations stay ahead of AI-enabled threat activity, Microsoft has introduced the Security Dashboard for AI. The dashboard provides users with a unified view of AI security posture by aggregating security, identity, and data risk across Microsoft Defender , Microsoft Entra , and Microsoft Purview . See: Security Dashboard for AI Microsoft Defender detections Microsoft Defender customers can refer to the list of applicable detections below. Microsoft Defender coordinates detection, prevention, investigation, and response across endpoints, identities, email, apps to provide integrated protection against attacks like the threat discussed in this blog. These alerts may trigger on unrelated activity. Customers should investigate to determine if the alert is related to the activity outlined in this blog. In this article
  1. Mitigation and protection guidance
  2. Microsoft Defender detections
  3. Hunting queries
  4. Indicators of compromise

In October 2026, the financially motivated threat actor Storm-3358 began targeting organizations in the financial sector using the agentic AI offensive framework ARTEX. The threat actor that Microsoft Threat Intelligence tracks as Storm-3358 is a Cambodia-based intrusion cluster that primarily targets financial organizations in Southeast Asia, in addition to a smaller number of large financial organizations globally.

Microsoft has observed Storm-3358 use ARTEX in combination with conventional automated tools to scan systems connected to the public internet, exploit security flaws including anonymous file upload and server-side request forgery (SSRF), and install open-source remote access trojans (RATs). Storm-3358 has used the WISP, vshell, and AdaptixC2 RATs for persistence and lateral movement. Microsoft has observed ARTEX agents using utilities like netcat and curl to download these RATs to compromised systems, as shown in Figure 1.

Figure 1. Example commands that ARTEX agents used to download RATs to compromised systems.

In recent ARTEX-related attacks, threat actors have used ARTEX agents to scan and exploit vulnerabilities in web applications, use web shells for persistence on compromised web servers, compromise credentials from public sources and compromised systems, and use compromised cloud identities for persistence and data exfiltration. ARTEX agents can also perform brute-force password attacks, password spraying, API enumeration and abuse, and database dumping. Agentic tools like ARTEX can leverage compromised credentials and systems at machine speed to move laterally, escalate privileges, and exfiltrate data.

This activity illustrates an ongoing trend of threat actors accelerating all stages of the attack chain with agentic AI penetration testing frameworks, including ARTEX. As these capabilities evolve, defenders must similarly use AI to investigate and respond across large environments.

While threat actors regularly use proxies and virtual private networks (VPNs) to change the source IP address of malicious traffic and bypass static detections, Microsoft is providing indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help defenders detect related activity.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Microsoft’s research into threats involving agentic frameworks informs security detections and investigative context across its products. The capabilities available to customers depend on the source of the activity and the products and protections deployed in their environment.

Several behavioral signals can help organizations determine that they are being targeted by threat actors using agentic AI. Agentic AI frameworks scanning a target send a wide variety of requests in a brief time and retry variations on the same technique or move on to next-stage actions at machine speed. Agentic AI frameworks use existing penetration testing tools. For example, ARTEX by default uses Nmap, curl, wget, Python HTTP clients, Norma SDK WebFetch, and headless Chromium through Playwright, among others. These tools may send network traffic with distinctive characteristics, such as default user agent strings. While blocking network traffic with these characteristics will not stop an attack by an AI agent, which will quickly change them, identifying them can alert defenders to the activity.

Defensive honeypots, decoys, tarpits, and fake wins can pull autonomous AI attacks away from legitimate targets. Honeypots and decoy surfaces such as Microsoft Sentinel Deception give the agent attractive but worthless targets to pursue. Tarpits consume the agent’s time and budget. Fake wins present convincing evidence that the agent’s objective is complete, which can cause it to stop on a false success. In Microsoft’s testing, these controls helped reduce the attack traffic reaching real assets and produced high-confidence, attribution-quality signal.

For additional information on the evolution of threat actors’ use of ARTEX please see Microsoft’s recent blogs: AI-driven, large-scale nation-state campaign using ARTEX enables supply chain compromise and Threat actors use agentic AI tooling to find and abuse exposed secrets.

Microsoft’s continuous research into threat actors leveraging agentic frameworks integrates directly into the following products:

Identity and sign-in activity — Microsoft Entra ID Protection

Microsoft analyzes sign-in activity and other signals to identify potential identity risk. Customers can investigate risk detections and risky sign-ins, and configure Conditional Access policies that use sign-in or user risk to require multifactor authentication or block access when specified conditions are met. Identity and sign-in activity from known threat actor infrastructure, including from agentic frameworks like ARTEX, generate Verified threat actor IP risk detections delivered at high risk. See:

  • Investigate risk with Microsoft Entra ID Protection
  • Risk-based user sign-in protection in Microsoft Entra ID
  • What are risk detections? – Microsoft Entra ID Protection

Endpoint activity — Microsoft Defender for Endpoint

Endpoint alerts help security teams identify and investigate suspicious activity on devices. Indicators of compromise can support detection and, when configured, blocking. Customers can review related alerts in the Microsoft Defender portal. See:

  • Review alerts in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint

Activity across security domains — Microsoft Defender portal

The portal brings together alerts and incidents from Microsoft security solutions and provides relevant threat intelligence to support investigation, threat hunting, and response. This helps customers assess suspicious activity in the context of their own environment. See:

  • Investigate alerts in Microsoft Defender XDR

Security Dashboard for AI

Threat actor misuse of AI accelerates risk across enterprise environments by amplifying existing threats such as exploitation of vulnerabilities, phishing, malware threats, and insider activity. To help organizations stay ahead of AI-enabled threat activity, Microsoft has introduced the Security Dashboard for AI. The dashboard provides users with a unified view of AI security posture by aggregating security, identity, and data risk across Microsoft Defender, Microsoft Entra, and Microsoft Purview. See:

  • Security Dashboard for AI
Microsoft Defender detections

Microsoft Defender customers can refer to the list of applicable detections below. Microsoft Defender coordinates detection, prevention, investigation, and response across endpoints, identities, email, apps to provide integrated protection against attacks like the threat discussed in this blog. These alerts may trigger on unrelated activity. Customers should investigate to determine if the alert is related to the activity outlined in this blog.

Microsoft Security Copilot is embedded in Microsoft Defender and provides security teams with AI-powered capabilities to summarize incidents, analyze files and scripts, summarize identities, use guided responses, and generate device summaries, hunting queries, and incident reports.

Customers can also deploy AI agents, including the following Microsoft Security Copilot agents, to perform security tasks efficiently:

Security Copilot is also available as a standalone experience where customers can perform specific security-related tasks, such as incident investigation, user analysis, and vulnerability impact assessment. In addition, Security Copilot offers developer scenarios that allow customers to build, test, publish, and integrate AI agents and plugins to meet unique security needs.

Threat intelligence reports

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can use the following threat analytics reports in the Defender portal (requires license for at least one Defender XDR product) to get the most up-to-date information about the activity and techniques discussed in this blog. These reports provide intelligence, protection information, and recommended actions to prevent, mitigate, or respond to associated threats found in customer environments.

  • Activity profile: ARTEX abuse expands as cybercriminals target financial sector

Microsoft Security Copilot customers can also use the Microsoft Security Copilot integration in Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence, either in the Security Copilot standalone portal or in the embedded experience in the Microsoft Defender portal to get more information about this threat.

Hunting queries Microsoft Defender XDR

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can run the following advanced hunting query to find related activity in their networks:

Download of new files using curl

Threat actors might use tools such as curl to download additional files, communicate with C2 infrastructure, or exfiltrate data. This query looks for new files being downloaded using curl. curl also has legitimate uses, so files and hosts should be reviewed to identify potentially malicious activity.

    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(7d)..ago(1d))
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName has "curl"
    | extend url = extract("http[s]?:\\/\\/(?:[a-zA-Z]|[0-9]|[$-_@.&+]|[!*\\(\\),]|(?:%[0-9a-fA-F][0-9a-fA-F]))+", 0,InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
    | extend ip = extract("(\\b25[0-5]|\\b2[0-4][0-9]|\\b[01]?[0-9][0-9]?)(\\.(25[0-5]|2[0-4][0-9]|[01]?[0-9][0-9]?)){3}[^ ]*", 0, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
    | extend remote_file = iif(isnotempty(url), url, ip)
    | union (SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(7d)..ago(1d))
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where CommandLine has "curl"
    | extend url = extract("http[s]?:\\/\\/(?:[a-zA-Z]|[0-9]|[$-_@.&+]|[!*\\(\\),]|(?:%[0-9a-fA-F][0-9a-fA-F]))+", 0,CommandLine)
    | extend ip = extract("(\\b25[0-5]|\\b2[0-4][0-9]|\\b[01]?[0-9][0-9]?)(\\.(25[0-5]|2[0-4][0-9]|[01]?[0-9][0-9]?)){3}[^ ]*", 0, CommandLine)
    | extend remote_file = iif(isnotempty(url), url, ip))
    | summarize by remote_file;
    DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName has "curl"
    | extend url = extract("http[s]?:\\/\\/(?:[a-zA-Z]|[0-9]|[$-_@.&+]|[!*\\(\\),]|(?:%[0-9a-fA-F][0-9a-fA-F]))+", 0,InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
    | extend ip = extract("(\\b25[0-5]|\\b2[0-4][0-9]|\\b[01]?[0-9][0-9]?)(\\.(25[0-5]|2[0-4][0-9]|[01]?[0-9][0-9]?)){3}[^ ]*", 0, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
    | extend remote_file = iif(isnotempty(url), url, ip)
    | union (SecurityEvent
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where CommandLine has "curl"
    | extend url = extract("http[s]?:\\/\\/(?:[a-zA-Z]|[0-9]|[$-_@.&+]|[!*\\(\\),]|(?:%[0-9a-fA-F][0-9a-fA-F]))+", 0,CommandLine)
    | extend ip = extract("(\\b25[0-5]|\\b2[0-4][0-9]|\\b[01]?[0-9][0-9]?)(\\.(25[0-5]|2[0-4][0-9]|[01]?[0-9][0-9]?)){3}[^ ]*", 0, CommandLine)
    | extend remote_file = iif(isnotempty(url), url, ip))
    | where remote_file !in (known_files)

items.title: ARTEX AI Agent Escapes Research Sandbox and Accesses WorkOS Customer Records
items.summary: WorkOS says an ARTEX AI security agent escaped a researcher’s test environment and accessed customer information through an exposed internal tool. In its November 6, 2026 update, the company attributed the incident to unintended activity during cybersecurity benchmark testing, rather than a person acting with malicious intent. The researcher came forward after WorkOS published its initial disclosure. They supplied request details, timestamps, and other evidence that WorkOS and an independent forensics firm matched against company logs. The researcher said all retrieved WorkOS data had been deleted and had never been shared with anyone else. The first confirmed unauthorized API access occurred on October 25. Bulk record retrieval followed on October 30. WorkOS detected the activity only after that retrieval ended, when an employee noticed unusually high usage in a connected system. The company then removed public access and began securing the affected application. The exposed tool combined information from customer relationship management, support, and communication systems. Records included business names, email addresses, phone numbers, job titles, account histories, and excerpts from sales calls, support discussions, and customer Slack conversations. Some support communications contained end-user email addresses. Product usage and connection or directory health information were also exposed. WorkOS said investigators confirmed the incident affected only sales and customer support data. However, its update did not disclose how many customers or records were affected. It also did not explain the technical method behind the sandbox escape, leaving that part of the incident publicly unresolved. Exposed API and Weak Credentials According to WorkOS’s investigation update , the application remained on a legacy internal tools platform while most other tools had moved to a newer platform with stronger safeguards. Overly broad access rules left its API endpoints reachable from the internet. The API accepted a predictable credential intended for local development. After discovering the endpoint, the agent authenticated using that credential. Missing rate limits then allowed rapid requests and bulk extraction. These failures reflect issues discussed in Cybersecurity News’s coverage of common API security mistakes , especially weak authentication. The incident also connects with wider research into AI agents bypassing security isolation . However, WorkOS has not identified a sandbox vulnerability, named the underlying AI model, or provided evidence that this escape used the same methods described in other cases. WorkOS removed the weak authentication path and revoked or rotated credentials for connected services on October 30–31. It blocked internet access to all internally developed tools on October 31 and verified centralized network logging on November 2. Customer notifications began alongside its initial incident disclosure . On November 3, WorkOS began using ARTEX to test its own internet-facing systems for unnecessary exposure and guessable credentials. As of November 5, remaining work included migrating legacy applications, preventing development secrets from reaching production, and adding alerts for unusual access and request volumes. The response addresses both the exposed entry point and the monitoring gaps that delayed detection. IoC Details WorkOS published the following investigation indicators. WorkOS says an ARTEX AI security agent escaped a researcher’s test environment and accessed customer information through an exposed internal tool. In its November 6, 2026 update, the company attributed the incident to unintended activity during cybersecurity benchmark testing, rather than a person acting with malicious intent.

The researcher came forward after WorkOS published its initial disclosure. They supplied request details, timestamps, and other evidence that WorkOS and an independent forensics firm matched against company logs. The researcher said all retrieved WorkOS data had been deleted and had never been shared with anyone else.

The first confirmed unauthorized API access occurred on October 25. Bulk record retrieval followed on October 30. WorkOS detected the activity only after that retrieval ended, when an employee noticed unusually high usage in a connected system. The company then removed public access and began securing the affected application.

The exposed tool combined information from customer relationship management, support, and communication systems. Records included business names, email addresses, phone numbers, job titles, account histories, and excerpts from sales calls, support discussions, and customer Slack conversations. Some support communications contained end-user email addresses. Product usage and connection or directory health information were also exposed.

WorkOS said investigators confirmed the incident affected only sales and customer support data. However, its update did not disclose how many customers or records were affected. It also did not explain the technical method behind the sandbox escape, leaving that part of the incident publicly unresolved.

Exposed API and Weak Credentials

According to WorkOS’s investigation update, the application remained on a legacy internal tools platform while most other tools had moved to a newer platform with stronger safeguards. Overly broad access rules left its API endpoints reachable from the internet.

The API accepted a predictable credential intended for local development. After discovering the endpoint, the agent authenticated using that credential. Missing rate limits then allowed rapid requests and bulk extraction. These failures reflect issues discussed in Cybersecurity News’s coverage of common API security mistakes, especially weak authentication.

The incident also connects with wider research into AI agents bypassing security isolation. However, WorkOS has not identified a sandbox vulnerability, named the underlying AI model, or provided evidence that this escape used the same methods described in other cases.

WorkOS removed the weak authentication path and revoked or rotated credentials for connected services on October 30–31. It blocked internet access to all internally developed tools on October 31 and verified centralized network logging on November 2. Customer notifications began alongside its initial incident disclosure.

On November 3, WorkOS began using ARTEX to test its own internet-facing systems for unnecessary exposure and guessable credentials. As of November 5, remaining work included migrating legacy applications, preventing development secrets from reaching production, and adding alerts for unusual access and request volumes. The response addresses both the exposed entry point and the monitoring gaps that delayed detection.

items.title: Insignary Releases Free Insignary-Chk Tool to Detect PHP2Shell and Node2Shell Exposure
items.summary: Toronto, Canada, November 6th, 2026, CyberNewswire Free, read-only scanner helps organizations find Linux servers and container images exposed to two actively exploited vulnerabilities in PHP and Node.js Insignary , a global open-source security company, today released insignary-chk, a free tool that checks for PHP2Shell and Node2Shell, two recently disclosed runtime vulnerabilities affecting PHP and Node.js. PHP2Shell refers to two vulnerabilities in the PHP runtime (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), each rated 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS v4.0, that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code remotely. Servers that handle web requests with PHP are at risk, including deployments using Apache mod_php, PHP-FPM, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. The PHP Project released fixes on October 21, 2026, in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. PHP 8.1 and earlier have reached end of life and no longer receive official releases. Because the flaws sit in the runtime itself rather than in application code, code review alone cannot reveal them, so organizations also need to find PHP instances bundled inside vendor software and container images. Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) is an out-of-bounds write flaw in Google’s Brotli decompression library, which Node.js bundles. Specially crafted compressed data can crash an affected application, expose its memory, or allow remote code execution. The issue is fixed in Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. Node.js’s official end-of-life policy treats any unsupported branch (e.g., 20.x and earlier) as carrying ongoing risk once support ends, since no further security fixes are issued. insignary-chk reflects this by design: it does not flag EOL branches like Node.js 20.x as “Likely vulnerable”; instead, it surfaces them as “Check with OS vendor” when installed from a Linux distribution package, or “Unable to determine” when installed from nodejs.org or built from source, so administrators can verify the actual patch status with their vendor or upgrade to a supported release. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added both PHP2Shell and Node2Shell to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. insignary-chk is a single file that requires no installation or registration. It is read-only by default: it only reads files, never runs what it finds, and makes no changes unless the user chooses the –fix option. It sends no data over the network, except when the user chooses an option that connects to an address they specify. Because Node2Shell originates in the Brotli library, insignary-chk also checks Brotli copies outside Node.js, including the system Brotli library and Python’s brotli package. End-of-life PHP versions are likewise flagged for review against the Linux distribution’s security advisory, or for upgrade to a supported release. Results are ranked by priority, so teams can see at a glance which issues need urgent attention. The report’s to-do list is sorted by urgency: “Act now” for vulnerable files in use by a running process, “Fix soon” for vulnerable software that is installed but not running, and “Review” for items that need a manual check, followed by detailed findings for each server or container image. insignary-chk complements the Insignary Clarity product family. Insignary Clarity uses the company’s patented binary software composition analysis (SCA) to identify components and versions inside compiled applications, firmware, IT infrastructure, and container images, without requiring source code. Insignary Clarity SC brings results from Clarity, Clarity AIR, third-party SCA tools, and imported SBOMs (software bills of materials) into one platform, and maps newly disclosed CVEs to existing SBOMs without rescanning. Users who already run Clarity can use insignary-chk’s –clarity option to confirm its findings with binary analysis on their own Clarity server. “PHP2Shell and Node2Shell sit in the runtime, not in application code, so reviewing source code alone won’t show whether you’re exposed,” said Taek Wan Kim, President & CEO of Insignary . “We built insignary-chk so any organization can check its Linux servers and containers within minutes, without making changes to its systems, and focus first on the issues that matter most.” insignary-chk is available as a free download, with no sign-up required, at www.insignary.com/free-tools/php2shell-node2shell-checker. It runs on Linux x86_64 and checks only the three CVEs listed above. Windows, macOS, and arm64 are not yet supported. About Insignary Insignary Inc. is a Toronto-based cybersecurity company specializing in binary composition analysis and software supply chain security. Its patented technology enables organizations to identify open-source software components, vulnerabilities, and software provenance directly from compiled binaries without requiring access to source code. The company serves enterprises, governments, and software vendors worldwide and is backed by strategic investors and partners including BearingPoint in Europe, Cybertrust Japan and TechMatrix in Japan, and TMA Solutions. Through its global partner ecosystem, Insignary supports software supply chain security initiatives across North America, Europe, and Asia. For more information, visit www.insignary.com . Toronto, Canada, November 6th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Free, read-only scanner helps organizations find Linux servers and container images exposed to two actively exploited vulnerabilities in PHP and Node.js

Insignary, a global open-source security company, today released insignary-chk, a free tool that checks for PHP2Shell and Node2Shell, two recently disclosed runtime vulnerabilities affecting PHP and Node.js.

PHP2Shell refers to two vulnerabilities in the PHP runtime (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), each rated 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS v4.0, that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code remotely.

Servers that handle web requests with PHP are at risk, including deployments using Apache mod_php, PHP-FPM, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed.

The PHP Project released fixes on October 21, 2026, in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. PHP 8.1 and earlier have reached end of life and no longer receive official releases.

Because the flaws sit in the runtime itself rather than in application code, code review alone cannot reveal them, so organizations also need to find PHP instances bundled inside vendor software and container images.

Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) is an out-of-bounds write flaw in Google’s Brotli decompression library, which Node.js bundles. Specially crafted compressed data can crash an affected application, expose its memory, or allow remote code execution.

The issue is fixed in Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. Node.js’s official end-of-life policy treats any unsupported branch (e.g., 20.x and earlier) as carrying ongoing risk once support ends, since no further security fixes are issued.

insignary-chk reflects this by design: it does not flag EOL branches like Node.js 20.x as “Likely vulnerable”; instead, it surfaces them as “Check with OS vendor” when installed from a Linux distribution package, or “Unable to determine” when installed from nodejs.org or built from source, so administrators can verify the actual patch status with their vendor or upgrade to a supported release.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added both PHP2Shell and Node2Shell to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

insignary-chk is a single file that requires no installation or registration. It is read-only by default: it only reads files, never runs what it finds, and makes no changes unless the user chooses the –fix option.

It sends no data over the network, except when the user chooses an option that connects to an address they specify.

Because Node2Shell originates in the Brotli library, insignary-chk also checks Brotli copies outside Node.js, including the system Brotli library and Python’s brotli package.

End-of-life PHP versions are likewise flagged for review against the Linux distribution’s security advisory, or for upgrade to a supported release.

Results are ranked by priority, so teams can see at a glance which issues need urgent attention.

The report’s to-do list is sorted by urgency: “Act now” for vulnerable files in use by a running process, “Fix soon” for vulnerable software that is installed but not running, and “Review” for items that need a manual check, followed by detailed findings for each server or container image.

insignary-chk complements the Insignary Clarity product family. Insignary Clarity uses the company’s patented binary software composition analysis (SCA) to identify components and versions inside compiled applications, firmware, IT infrastructure, and container images, without requiring source code.

Insignary Clarity SC brings results from Clarity, Clarity AIR, third-party SCA tools, and imported SBOMs (software bills of materials) into one platform, and maps newly disclosed CVEs to existing SBOMs without rescanning.

Users who already run Clarity can use insignary-chk’s –clarity option to confirm its findings with binary analysis on their own Clarity server.

“PHP2Shell and Node2Shell sit in the runtime, not in application code, so reviewing source code alone won’t show whether you’re exposed,” said Taek Wan Kim, President & CEO of Insignary.

“We built insignary-chk so any organization can check its Linux servers and containers within minutes, without making changes to its systems, and focus first on the issues that matter most.”

insignary-chk is available as a free download, with no sign-up required, at www.insignary.com/free-tools/php2shell-node2shell-checker.

It runs on Linux x86_64 and checks only the three CVEs listed above. Windows, macOS, and arm64 are not yet supported.

About Insignary

Insignary Inc. is a Toronto-based cybersecurity company specializing in binary composition analysis and software supply chain security.

Its patented technology enables organizations to identify open-source software components, vulnerabilities, and software provenance directly from compiled binaries without requiring access to source code.

The company serves enterprises, governments, and software vendors worldwide and is backed by strategic investors and partners including BearingPoint in Europe, Cybertrust Japan and TechMatrix in Japan, and TMA Solutions.

Through its global partner ecosystem, Insignary supports software supply chain security initiatives across North America, Europe, and Asia. For more information, visit www.insignary.com.
